name: Mbed TLS
baseline: OpenSSL 3.6.0 EVP one-shot AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305
workload: Google Benchmark of one-shot AEAD encryption of a 16-byte-AAD message, 64 to 16384 bytes, per call including key setup (Mbed TLS PSA psa_import_key plus psa_aead_encrypt; OpenSSL EVP_CIPHER_CTX_new, init, update, final, free), Mbed TLS 4.0.0 vs OpenSSL 3.6.0 built from source and statically linked in the scc-tw/cryptobench-cpp suite.
claimed_speedup: Only at the 64-byte message size, means of 5 repetitions: AES-128-GCM 211.7 vs 163.9 MB/s (1.29x), AES-256-GCM 197.0 vs 160.9 MB/s (1.22x), ChaCha20-Poly1305 168.5 vs 135.3 MB/s (1.25x) (all derived from page data: bytes_per_second / 1e6). The ranking flips from 256 bytes up: OpenSSL is faster by 1.05x for AES-128-GCM at 256 B and by 4.7x at 16384 B (7840.4 vs 1683.0 MB/s), and OpenSSL wins every hash, HMAC and AES-256-CBC row where both libraries have data.
compiler_and_flags: README states -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto -funroll-loops -fomit-frame-pointer (PGO optional) applied to all libraries; result.json records no compiler name, version or PGO state. Mbed TLS 4.0.0 (tag v4.0.0) is built with its default configuration, static, via cmake/FetchMbedTLS.cmake.
hardware: MacBook Air host 'sccdeMacBook-Air.local' (Apple Silicon implied by the cache sizes; chip model not named), 8 logical CPUs, 64 KB L1D, 128 KB L1I, 4 MB L2 in the result.json context block; single run dated 2025-11-05.
tradeoffs: Mbed TLS targets small code size and portability, not peak throughput. The 64-byte win comes with a PSA API that imports a key per call; for messages of 1 KB and up OpenSSL is 1.7x to 4.7x faster for GCM, 2.5x to 3.8x faster for ChaCha20-Poly1305 and 5.7x to 7.5x faster for SHA-256 in the same run (all derived from page data).
caveats: Harvested shootout row, not a claim Mbed TLS makes: the README and ChangeLog contain no comparison with OpenSSL, and Mbed TLS is the slower library for every hash, HMAC and CBC row and for AEAD at 256 B and above. The benchmark owner's repo (scc-tw/cryptobench-cpp) has 0 stars and 39 commits, one local laptop run, no CPU model or compiler version, so it is capped at C (same tier the wave 7 verifier gave this source for libsodium BLAKE2b). The 64-byte advantage probably reflects OpenSSL 3 per-call overhead rather than cipher speed: the OpenSSL AES-GCM adapter allocates and frees an EVP_CIPHER_CTX and runs the init calls on every message (the Mbed TLS adapter also imports a PSA key and allocates a std::vector per call). In the same file every OpenSSL public-key row and Botan's AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-256-CBC rows are error rows ('Encryption failed' and similar), so OpenSSL is the only peer for this comparison. A wolfSSL vendor benchmark (WebSearch snippet only, page not opened) reports wolfCrypt well ahead of Mbed TLS 3.6.6; no source reached shows Mbed TLS ahead of OpenSSL on bulk throughput.

name: GnuPG (gpg)
workload: Public-key encryption of a 1 GiB stream of /dev/urandom (dd bs=1M count=1024) to one recipient, compression off, piped through bar to /dev/null, in ASCII-armored and in binary output mode: gpg --always-trust -er foo --compress-algo none [--armor] vs sq encrypt --recipient-cert foo.pub --compression none [--binary].
claimed_speedup: Binary output: gpg 170.7 MB/s (6 s) vs sq 128.0 MB/s (8 s), 1.33x (derived from page data). ASCII-armored output: gpg 138.7 MB/s (10 s) vs sq 51.4 MB/s (27 s), 2.70x (derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 991 stars on the GitHub mirror (maintainers do not track the mirror; canonical repo is git.gnupg.org, not opened)
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0-or-later (copyleft), so code cannot be copied into permissive projects; the evidence covers only streaming public-key encryption, not signing, verification or key management.
caveats: Single anonymous snippet of terminal output in a Sequoia bug titled 'Sequoia's encryption is slow compared to GnuPG's': the page shows no author, date, gpg or sq versions, key type, cipher or packet format, CPU, or maintainer reply, so tier C (numbers without methodology). The pipeline includes dd reading /dev/urandom, which can itself cap throughput near the quoted figures, and the armored gap includes sq's encoder cost, so this is not a clean cipher-speed comparison. It is a claim made against Sequoia, not by GnuPG. GnuPG's own NEWS (raw.githubusercontent.com/gpg/gnupg/HEAD/NEWS) lists only self-versus-earlier-release speedups: signature verification more than four times faster, detached signing doubled, threefold decryption speedup for large files, AES256.OCB encryption nearly doubled. Those have no named external baseline. Suggested category was signatures-kem; encryption throughput fits aead-and-ciphers better.
